analysis.one_liner: Replaces state product liability laws with uniform federal rules that make it harder to sue product makers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 1989 with 23 Republican cosponsors, was referred to House subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the patchwork of state product liability laws with a single federal set of rules covering any lawsuit over an injury or damage caused by a product. It would have made federal safety compliance a near-complete defense, barred punitive damages for federally approved drugs, medical devices, and aircraft, shortened the deadline for filing suit to two years, and cut off claims against many older products entirely. The stated goal was to reduce manufacturers' litigation costs and insurance uncertainty; the practical effect would have been to make it much harder for injured people to recover from product makers and sellers.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, product sellers, and product liability insurers would gain if the bill passed. Manufacturers would avoid liability for designs and warnings unless safer alternatives were reasonably knowable at the time of manufacture, and compliance with any federal safety standard would be treated as conclusive proof of no defect [S3]. Drug and device makers would be shielded from punitive damages for products approved by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and aircraft makers from punitive damages for FAA-certified planes, unless they hid or misrepresented information to regulators [S3]. Retailers and other sellers would be liable only if the injured person proved the seller itself was negligent, rather than being held responsible for a defective product simply for selling it [S2][S3]. General aviation makers would be protected from suits over aircraft more than 12 years old [S3]. The bill's stated purposes include letting insurers base rates on predictable, uniform liability standards [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would supersede state product liability law whenever it provides a rule on recovery, creating one uniform federal standard in place of stricter state laws [S2][S3].

A manufacturer or seller would not be liable for a design or warning defect if the product met federal standards at the time it was made, and an agency finding of compliance would be conclusive evidence — claimants could overcome it only by showing a reasonable person would have taken additional precautions [S3].

Punitive damages would be barred against makers of FDA-approved drugs and medical devices and FAA-certified aircraft unless the company withheld or misrepresented material safety information to regulators, and would require clear and convincing evidence of flagrant indifference to safety even in other cases [S3].

All product liability suits would have to be filed within two years of when the harm was or should have been discovered, with claims against capital goods and general aviation aircraft barred after 12 years regardless of discovery [S3].

Product sellers would be liable only if the injured person proved the seller's own lack of reasonable care caused the harm, removing sellers' traditional responsibility for defective products they placed in commerce [S2][S3].

Manufacturers would bear no liability for harm from unforeseeable misuse, alterations, or dangers obvious to ordinary users, and no liability at all if the injured person was under the influence of alcohol or unprescribed drugs and that condition was more than 50 percent responsible [S3].

Each defendant would pay only its own percentage share of damages rather than being jointly responsible for the full award, and any damages award would be reduced by workers' compensation benefits paid for the same injury [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products, and their families, would bear the cost. They would face a two-year filing deadline with no exceptions for slowly developing harm except toxic exposure cases [S3], lose access to sellers as defendants when the manufacturer is hard to reach [S3], be barred from suing over products covered by federal standards unless they could prove more precautions were warranted [S3], be unable to collect punitive damages from makers of approved drugs, devices, and certified aircraft [S3], and see awards reduced by the workers' compensation benefits they were already owed [S3]. Anyone hurt by a 12-year-old aircraft or capital good would have no claim at all [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's defenders would say uniform national standards reduce the uncertainty that raises insurance costs and discourages product innovation, and that states could still develop alternative dispute-resolution systems consistent with the federal rules [S3].

Treating a federal agency's compliance finding as conclusive evidence would let companies rely on regulator approval as a shield even where the standard was outdated or less protective than a reasonable manufacturer's own judgment, with recourse for injured people only through the narrow 'additional precautions' exception [S3].

The two-year deadline and 12-year cutoffs would eliminate valid claims — for example, injuries from long-serving aircraft parts — that state law in many states would still allow, with no exception for harms discovered late [S3].

Eliminating joint liability would leave an injured person holding the loss whenever one responsible defendant is insolvent, judgment-proof, or beyond the court's reach, except where the manufacturer is unreachable and the seller is treated as the manufacturer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill is predictability: one federal rulebook instead of fifty state systems, and less exposure to unpredictable jury awards, which its drafters argued would lower costs for manufacturers and consumers alike [S3]. But the specific protections are drafted heavily toward defendants — conclusive evidentiary weight for regulatory compliance, a punitive damages bar for entire regulated industries, short deadlines, and a workers' compensation offset that reduces an injured worker's recovery [S3]. An honest supporter would have to concede that the savings to industry would come largely out of payments to people hurt by defective products, and the bill's death without any hearing suggests even its backers saw no realistic path in a Congress where it had no Democratic support.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, which passed it down to subcommittees that never acted on it, and it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Ritter introduced the bill on March 23, 1989, joined by 23 Republican cosponsors; all 24 supporters were House Republicans [S1][S4].
The House referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees the day it was introduced [S5].
Within three weeks it was sent down to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the April 10, 1989 subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products are better off, because they kept the full range of state-law rights to sue manufacturers and sellers that the bill would have preempted. Manufacturers, insurers, and aviation makers did not get the liability shields they sought, and the plaintiffs' bar kept the legal landscape it practices in.

for.name: Rep. Don Ritter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Uniform Product Liability Act of 1989 and recruited the bill's original cosponsors.

for.name: 23 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

for.name: Manufacturers and product liability insurers
for.role: Industry coalition backing federal product liability standards
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress through the 1980s for federal uniform product liability standards, citing unpredictable jury awards and rising liability insurance costs; the bill's own stated purposes echo their position, including letting insurers rate on uniform standards.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee on the day of introduction, which never acted further.

against.name: Jack Brooks
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee, which never reported it back.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican (24 of 175), and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in a House run by a 257-seat Democratic majority, so the fight never reached a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Manufacturers (including drug, medical device, and aviation makers)
industries.note: The bill would give manufacturers a federal shield: compliance with government standards becomes conclusive evidence against design and warning claims, punitive damages are barred for approved drugs, devices, and certified aircraft, and liability for older products expires. These protections come directly at the expense of people injured by defective products.

The bill is explicitly designed to let insurers base rates on predictable, uniform liability standards [S3]. Lower claim frequency and smaller payouts would cut insurers' costs, but the savings mechanism is fewer and smaller recoveries for injured people.

Sellers would be liable only for their own proven negligence or breach of their own express warranty, ending the traditional rule that made anyone who sold a defective product responsible for it [S2][S3]. Injured buyers would lose a deep-pocket defendant when the manufacturer is unreachable, except in the narrow case where the seller is then treated as the manufacturer.

Preempting state tort law, shortening deadlines, and raising the bar for punitive damages would shrink the caseload and recoveries available in product liability work. Their interest in opposing the bill ran alongside their clients' ability to recover.
